annotationRationale: The central task is enforcing the exact interval represented by a floor value. The primary route bounds the integer part; the alternative uses integrality and parity to restrict the fractional part.

classificationReview.areaCheck: Algebra is correct; no repair is needed.

review.questionCheck: The solutions are \(2/3,1,2,11/3\), giving four distinct values and choice B. The prompt, choices and key agree with the supplied references. No problem figure or grading conflict is present.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: The bounded floor-value search and fractional-part parity argument provide useful distinct routes. The supplied graphical methods largely visualize the same interval analysis and need not be added.
review.annotationCheck: Floor and fractional-part reasoning is correctly assessed. Quadratic inequalities, parity and factoring are appropriately attached to the individual methods rather than forced into shared question support.
review.areaCheck: Algebra is correct; no repair is needed.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The equation forces \(x\ge2/3\), hence a nonnegative floor n. The strict upper floor bound gives \(n(n-3)<1\), excluding every n at least 4. Testing n=0,1,2,3 verifies both floor endpoints for all four stated candidates. Each floor determines one x, so the count is exhaustive.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: The LIVE substitution and interval constraints support the route, and AoPS Solution 1 supplies a finite-search perspective. The candidate replaces that solution's informal growth claim with an explicit bound and uses independently developed explanatory prose.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The explanation motivates the integer substitution, proves the finite search bound and checks the required half-open intervals. No graph or additional prerequisite is needed.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: math:floor-ceiling captures the endpoint-sensitive consistency condition. cnm_h024 fits restricting the integer solutions of the resulting quadratic inequality.

nativeLayerJudgments.CN: The exact quadratic-inequality link supports the bound and integer restriction. The floor concept itself has no supplied CN link.
nativeLayerJudgments.US: Neither immediate node has a supplied US link. The floor reasoning should remain an acknowledged competition-skill alignment gap.
nativeLayerJudgments.ailleo: Both direct IDs fit the actual derivation; the precise floor node carries the central concept.

methodReviews.mathCheck: With \(x=n+f\) and \(0\le f<1\), the equation becomes \((n-1)(n-2)=3f\). The product is an even integer in [0,3), so only 0 and 2 occur. Their factorizations give n=1,2 with f=0 and n=0,3 with f=2/3. All four satisfy the floor condition and are distinct.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: AoPS Solutions 6 and 11 support separating integer and fractional parts. Using consecutive-integer parity to eliminate the middle case is a valid original simplification. The third-party-informed classification and prose are appropriate.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The opening identifies why this decomposition helps. The consecutive-integer observation, exhaustive two-case split and final floor verification make the argument independently reconstructible.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: math:floor-ceiling, cnm_p156 and cnm_224 match the decomposition, parity restriction and zero-product solutions. The factoring node is used for equations, within its corrected scope.
